video_title: Are We In a Dating Recession? with Logan Ury
gist: Comedy-led interview in which Hasan Minhaj talks with Hinge's director of relationship science Logan Ury (spelled 'Logan Yuri' in the captions) about dating-app burnout, height filters, getting users off the app and onto in-person dates faster, the loneliness crisis and 'friction', and Gottman relationship research. There is little direct market content. The investor-relevant signal is consumer and social data on dating-app fatigue, Hinge's product positioning, and falling in-person socializing, which matters for the online-dating category (Match, Bumble) and for businesses built around in-person experiences.

insights.claim: Hasan Minhaj cites data showing that 53% of singles report dating burnout, with about the same share reporting loneliness, which suggests user fatigue is widespread across the online-dating category.
insights.speaker: Hasan Minhaj
insights.so_what: Burnout among singles is a headwind for engagement and paying-user retention at dating apps such as Match Group and Bumble. Watch user and payer trends.
insights.quote: 53% of singles say they are experiencing dating burnout

insights.claim: A Pew survey cited on the show found that 42% of US adults say online dating has made finding a long-term partner easier, so the apps' core usefulness is still widely recognized even as users complain about them.
insights.speaker: Hasan Minhaj
insights.so_what: Demand for the category is not structurally broken. The frustration is about the experience, and product changes could address it.
insights.quote: 42% of all US adults said that online dating made the search for a long-term partner easier

insights.claim: Too much choice is both the main benefit and the main problem of dating apps: they reduce people to a few desirability metrics, men report getting no matches, and women report harassment.
insights.speaker: Hasan Minhaj
insights.so_what: Apps that cut choice overload (curation, fewer and better matches) may hold users better than apps built only for swipe volume.
insights.quote: one of their biggest benefits is also their biggest problem. They have created so much choice. It's overwhelming.

insights.claim: Hinge markets itself as 'the app designed to be deleted', so its brand rests on successful exits rather than on engagement, which runs against the usual consumer-app model.
insights.speaker: Hasan Minhaj
insights.so_what: Hinge's positioning trades raw engagement for brand trust and word of mouth (two of the show's producers met their spouses on Hinge). Judge it on revenue per user, not time spent in the app.
insights.quote: They call themselves the app designed to be deleted.

insights.claim: Minhaj argues that dating's problems are mostly old (ghosting existed as 'not calling back') and that modern apps mainly add freedom, and the messiness that comes with it.
insights.speaker: Hasan Minhaj
insights.so_what: This pushes back on the 'dating recession' story: discontent may be cyclical and complaint-driven rather than a sign that the category is shrinking.
insights.quote: The problem with modern dating, these problems are real, but most of them aren't new.

insights.claim: Logan Ury says many women on dating apps set 6 feet as a minimum height, yet only 14% of US men are 6 feet or taller, so these filters hide about 86% of potential matches.
insights.speaker: Logan Ury
insights.so_what: Self-imposed filters shrink the pool users can match with and feed dissatisfaction. Product design around filters (deal-breaker versus preference) is a lever on match rates.
insights.quote: so many women on the apps put six feet as a height minimum. And only 14% of men in the US are six feet or taller.

insights.claim: Hinge research finds that about 3 days of chatting in the app is the right time to ask for a date. Ury wants users to leave the app and meet in person faster, because chemistry over text does not predict anything.
insights.speaker: Logan Ury
insights.so_what: Hinge treats the app as a 'modern matchmaker' whose success is measured by offline dates. This is a different product strategy from apps that maximize messaging engagement.
insights.quote: at Hinge, we found that after 3 days of chatting on the app is the right amount of time to then ask someone on a date

insights.claim: Hinge has spent about 10 years on profile research. Its guidance is an accurate, flattering headshot first, followed by a full-body shot, an activity, and friends or family, and it warns against 'kitten fishing' with old photos.
insights.speaker: Logan Ury
insights.so_what: Hinge's moat includes proprietary behavioral data on what drives matches, which it uses for user coaching and content marketing.

insights.claim: Hasan Minhaj cites a 2006 MIT study estimating that shorter men would need about $40,000 more income per inch of height to be as desirable to the women they want to date.
insights.speaker: Hasan Minhaj
insights.so_what: This gives a size to the height preference that dating-app filters lock in. It is mostly a curiosity, but it shows how much weight users put on a single filtered attribute.
insights.quote: it worked out to be approximately $40,000 per inch

themes.theme: Loneliness crisis and the case for friction

insights.claim: Logan Ury says that over the last 20 years adults have spent 30% less time with friends and teens 50% less, a 'hanging out crisis' she links to more comfortable homes and an addictive TikTok algorithm.
insights.speaker: Logan Ury
insights.so_what: A long-term drop in in-person socializing is a structural headwind for venues and social businesses, and an opening for products that create real-world connection.
insights.quote: in the last 20 years, adults are spending 30% less time hanging out with their friends and teens are spending 50% less time

insights.claim: Ury argues that convenience apps such as grocery delivery and online ordering remove the everyday 'friction' where people meet, so the loneliness crisis calls for adding friction back. She also says that the more money people have, the more isolated they become.
insights.speaker: Logan Ury
insights.so_what: This is a counter-narrative to the convenience economy. It points to a possible consumer swing toward in-person, community-based experiences (run clubs, hosted dinners, lines and events).
insights.quote: the more money you have, the more isolated you are

insights.claim: Shared discomfort, such as a 5-hour flight delay, works as an icebreaker. Ury says standing in lines and hosting events (dinners where each guest brings a single friend) are underrated ways to meet partners.
insights.speaker: Logan Ury
insights.so_what: This supports the case for event, hosting and IRL-community formats as alternatives or complements to swipe-based apps.
insights.quote: shared discomfort is actually the ultimate icebreaker

insights.claim: Ury cites the 'weak ties' research, which finds people more often get jobs, and by extension date introductions, through acquaintances than through close friends because acquaintances reach different social circles. She says workplaces were among the most common places couples met before dating apps.
insights.speaker: Logan Ury
insights.so_what: Remote work and shrinking social circles cut the weak-tie channels that apps and setup networks now try to replace.

insights.claim: Hasan Minhaj argues that remote work through email and Zoom means young people lose a major chance to meet others and learn basic social skills, adding to the feeling of being broke, isolated and stuck.
insights.speaker: Hasan Minhaj
insights.so_what: Remote work is a second-order driver of loneliness and of demand for dating apps.
insights.quote: Young people are feeling broke, isolated, and stuck. But they want to be in relationships.

insights.claim: Logan Ury says the top complaint women bring her about dates is 'ZQ', or zero questions. Research shows people like conversation partners who are interested more than ones who are interesting, so support responses beat shift responses.
insights.speaker: Logan Ury
insights.so_what: This is a behavioral insight Hinge turns into coaching content. It is useful context for how dating apps try to improve date quality and outcomes.
insights.quote: people are much more likely to like you if you are interested not interesting

insights.claim: Hinge research shows people would rather be rejected clearly than be ghosted or left in ambiguity, which supports product features that encourage closure.
insights.speaker: Logan Ury
insights.so_what: Features that cut ghosting may improve user sentiment and retention on dating platforms.
insights.quote: people would rather be rejected and understand where they stand than to be ghosted or to live in ambiguity

insights.claim: Ury hosts the Netflix show 'The Later Daters' (spelled 'Later Datator' in the captions) for daters over 55. She argues that longer lifespans mean widowed or divorced people at 60 may have decades of dating ahead, a growing over-55 market.
insights.speaker: Logan Ury
insights.so_what: Older singles are an underserved and growing segment for dating products and media.
insights.quote: you are widowed at 60, you have 40 more years for companionship and intimacy

insights.claim: In John Gottman's 'love lab' study of 131 couples, the couples still together and happy six years later turned toward their partner's bids for connection 86% of the time, against 33% for couples who broke up or stayed together unhappily.
insights.speaker: Logan Ury
insights.so_what: Small daily interactions predict whether a relationship lasts. Ury's view that great relationships are built, not discovered, shapes how Hinge frames success.
insights.quote: great relationships are built, they're not discovered

insights.claim: According to Gottman research cited by Ury, 69% of relationship problems are perpetual, so healthy couples learn to fight well rather than avoid conflict.
insights.speaker: Logan Ury
insights.so_what: This is context on relationship science and has little direct market relevance.
insights.quote: 69% of problems in relationships are perpetual
